title: Rivers to the sea
hook: the Tao in the world is like rivers flowing to the sea (Tao Te Ching 32)

segments.voice: Yesterday, victory as a funeral: the general standing with the mourners. Your line was win sadly. If you won something, did you look at the one who lost? Day one thousand ninety-four.

Rain hitting a roof doesn't decide where to go. It runs to the gutter, the gutter to the drain, the drain to a creek, the creek to a river. Nobody steers it. Nobody has to persuade a single drop. After two days of armies and weapons, chapter thirty-two of the Tao Te Ching turns to something much quieter: water going downhill, and dew settling on the ground. Its last line is the one in today's title, and it describes the Tao by the place where all the water ends up.
screen: `RAIN DOESN'T DECIDE WHERE TO GO.` → `NOBODY STEERS IT.` → `WHERE ALL THE WATER ENDS UP.`

segments.voice: First, the small thing nobody can master. The chapter opens by saying the Tao has no name. In its plain simplicity it may look small, and yet, it says, nobody in the world can make it a servant. Small is not the same as weak. Second, the dew. The chapter says heaven and earth come together and send down sweet dew, and the dew reaches everywhere evenly, of its own accord, without anyone giving orders. No official decides which field gets watered. It just falls, and it falls on all of them. Third, names and stopping. The chapter says that once things are shaped and divided, they get names, and once there are names, it's time to know where to stop. Legge's wording is that people can then know to rest in it, and so stay clear of failure. Some readers hear a warning in that: naming is useful, but endless sorting and labeling is where things go wrong. Fourth, the sea. The chapter closes, in James Legge's translation: "The relation of the Tao to all the world is like that of the great rivers and seas to the streams from the valleys." The streams aren't dragged to the sea. The sea doesn't chase them. They arrive because the sea is low and open, and water goes where it's received. It can be a picture of a person, too. Some people pull everyone toward them by force of personality. And some people are simply where others end up: the kitchen everyone drifts into at a party, the friend people call first. Not because they grabbed. Because there's room.
screen: `SMALL, AND NOBODY CAN MASTER IT.` · `THE DEW FALLS ON EVERY FIELD.` · `NAMES, AND KNOWING WHERE TO STOP.` · `STREAMS ARRIVE WHERE THEY'RE RECEIVED.` · then, large: `RIVERS TO THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: follow water with your eyes. If there's a window, a sink, a glass of water nearby, find it. If not, let your mind find some water you know: a creek, a gutter in the rain, the tap running. Watch it move. Notice that it never argues with the slope. It takes the next low place, and then the next, without hurrying and without stopping. Follow it as far as your eyes or your memory can go, and let your breath move at the same easy pace. The bell holds the time.
Rivers to the sea. Chapter thirty-two's closing picture: the Tao is to the world as the great rivers and seas are to the streams that run into them from the valleys. Today's word.
Your line: to the sea. Today, be the low, open place for one person: let them come to you and talk, and don't steer where it goes. Day one thousand ninety-four.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-two as a picture of influence without force: like the sea that streams flow into, the Tao draws things by being low and open rather than by pulling.

fork.reveal: the chapter compares the Tao to the great rivers and seas: the streams arrive on their own, because water goes to the low place.

trapdoor: what you thought: rivers to the sea is a pretty nature image.
what it means: the Tao draws things to it the way the sea receives streams, without pulling, because it is low and open.
what a scholar hears: the chapter's first line names 樸, the uncarved block, which Legge renders as primordial simplicity: the plain, unshaped state before names divide things.

notes: Check the Legge 1891 quotation of chapter 32's last sentence word for word.

Paraphrases of chapter 32: the Tao nameless and small in its simplicity, yet no one can treat it as a minister; heaven and earth sending down sweet dew that reaches everywhere equally of its own accord; once there are names, knowing to rest (Legge) and so avoiding failure. Other translators render this 'knowing when to stop'; the teach uses both. Confirm.
Day 1090 (Be the valley, chapter 28) also uses lowness; this day leads with the dew, names and the sea's receiving, to avoid repeating the valley image.
Trapdoor: 樸 in chapter 32 rendered by Legge as 'primordial simplicity'; confirm the gloss 'uncarved block'.
The kitchen and friend examples are the writer's illustrations.
